questions.q: What are the six sections of the benchmarking write-up template used in this lesson's worked example?
options: Hypothesis, experiment, oracle, diffusion, measurement, conclusion
Problem statement, classical baseline, quantum approach, experimental/verified numbers, honest caveats, bottom-line verdict
Title, abstract, body, figures, caveats, verdict
Introduction, methods, results, discussion, references, appendix
questions.explain: The template is specifically: problem statement, classical baseline, quantum approach, experimental/verified numbers, honest caveats, bottom-line verdict — in that order.

questions.q: In the worked example, what classical worst-case and average-case query counts are stated for N=8 unstructured search?
options: 2 worst case, 1 average case
8 worst case, 4.5 average case
4 worst case, 2 average case
16 worst case, 8 average case
questions.explain: The classical baseline section states 8 as the worst case (checking every item) and 4.5 as the average case, using the (N+1)/2 formula.

questions.q: Why does the worked example's 'Honest caveats' section note that N=8 might be too small a scale for a clean real-world comparison?
options: Because quantum hardware overhead (initialization, error correction, I/O) could dominate the raw query-count advantage at small N, making the comparison cleanest only at larger scale
Because classical computers cannot search spaces smaller than 100 items
Because Grover's algorithm doesn't work at all for N less than 100
Because the formula ⌊(π/4)√N⌋ is undefined for N=8
questions.explain: At small N, fixed overheads of running a quantum circuit can swamp a theoretical query-count advantage, which is why the caveat distinguishes asymptotic advantage from practical advantage at small scale.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the template structure 'forces completeness before conclusions'?
options: Because the template was designed by a committee and has no logical ordering

Because the bottom-line verdict section comes after the classical baseline and caveats sections, making it impossible to honestly state a verdict without having already accounted for the comparison and its limitations
Because the template requires a minimum word count for each section
Because the sections must be written in alphabetical order
questions.explain: The ordering means a writer must state the classical baseline and caveats before reaching the verdict, preventing an unsupported or overstated conclusion from standing on its own.

questions.q: What does the worked example's bottom-line verdict explicitly avoid claiming?
options: That classical computers can also achieve O(√N) query complexity
That the N=8 numbers were computed correctly
That Grover's algorithm provides any speedup at all
That quantum computers search faster 'in general', since the advantage depends on the absence of exploitable structure, real oracle cost, and low hardware error rates
questions.explain: The verdict is deliberately narrow: a real, verified quadratic reduction in oracle queries under stated conditions, not a blanket claim that quantum computers search faster in general.
